name: Cold-pressed oils / olive oil

lead: Cold-pressed oils, especially extra virgin olive oil, are made without heat or solvents and are promoted as alternatives to refined seed oils.
Regulators allow limited health claims about heart disease when olive oil replaces saturated fat; effects on appearance have not been established in the sources reviewed.

paras: The oil is rich in oleic acid and polyphenols, which are sensitive to heat, light and oxygen.
Few direct risks are reported; documented concerns involve fraud and mislabelling, and the FDA claim is described as limited and not conclusive.

Olive Oil Three Times Per Day?

lead: Cold-pressed oils, most prominently extra virgin olive oil, are edible oils extracted mechanically without heat or chemical solvents. In looksmaxxing and wider diet-culture discussion they are promoted as replacements for refined seed oils, with claims about skin and general health [1].

Extra virgin olive oil is the top grade under International Olive Council standards, requiring cold mechanical extraction and free acidity of no more than 0.8 percent [1]. In the US the FDA allows a qualified health claim that limited and not conclusive evidence suggests about two tablespoons daily may reduce coronary heart disease risk when replacing saturated fat [1].
infobox: Not examined in the sources reviewed

paras: Virgin oils are made by mechanical means only. Cold pressed generally means the oil was not heated above about 27 degrees Celsius, though the EU reserves that term for oil that is physically pressed rather than centrifuged, and the phrase first cold pressed has no reliable international definition [1].
Production involves crushing olives, stirring the paste, separating oil by pressing or centrifuge, and optional filtering. Refined and pomace oils involve chemical processing or solvents [1].

Olive oil is mostly monounsaturated oleic acid, with smaller amounts of linoleic and palmitic acid. Polyphenols make up about 0.5 percent and give the bitter, peppery taste but decline with heat, light and oxygen [1].

In 2011 the European Food Safety Authority supported claims that olive polyphenols protect blood lipids from oxidation and that replacing saturated fat with oleic acid helps maintain normal LDL cholesterol, but said cause and effect was not established for triglycerides, HDL cholesterol or blood glucose [1].

Ancient Greeks rubbed oil on the body during exercise, and cosmetic use began in the 7th century BC [1]. The sources reviewed for this article do not report clinical trials of dietary or topical olive oil for facial appearance.

Journalist Tom Mueller's reporting and 2011 book Extra Virginity alleged widespread mislabelling of extra virgin oil, and authorities have conducted enforcement operations in Italy and Spain, including arrests in 2008 and 2012. In July 2024 the EU reported record olive oil fraud cases [1].
No studies found on cold-pressed oils as a replacement for seed oils for appearance outcomes. Cardiovascular regulatory assessments are noted above [1].
